utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We found on our desk Exhibit P954 in B/C/S. I take it -- I don't know who presented that. I think it was the Prosecution. There might be no need to have everything translated, but at least to have relevant portions translated in such a way, for example, the headings in the lists, so that we could find our way through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll be glad to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then, Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures, as far as I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would mean your next witness would be Mr. Lazar Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, will you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I just say while the witness is coming in, Your Honour, we served a supplemental information sheet on the witness with a copy to the Chamber. That was only done quite early today, but as far as I understand, there's no -- certainly at the moment there's no issue that arises on that. I don't know whether Your Honours will have noticed that the estimate for the witness has been revised from two and a half to three and a half hours. Of course, it's only an estimate, Your Honour, and I -- well, nobody knows exactly how fast we get to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know. I can imagine that some of the personal history of the witness could be dealt with in a rather leading way, Mr. Harmon. I see you're nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There won't be much, Your Honour. I was proposing, actually, to lead through that and also through a certain amount of basic geography and facts about the municipality which seems to be much more conveniently dealt with leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stavnjak. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Stewart, counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're Mr. Lazar Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you're 47 years old, and until sometime in 1992, you had lived your whole life in Gorazde; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we'll go into some personal history at some point. But you were never a member of the Communist Party, were you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you currently live in Cajnice, where you were the deputy mayor with particular responsibility for business affairs?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Not the deputy, but an assistant to the mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you are also an elected member of the Municipal Assembly of Cajnice and the president of the Cajnice SDS Deputies Club?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And your post as an assistant mayor, as it's been translated, is a paid post; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that's your sole employment at the moment, is it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So in fact you have -- your personal qualifications are in mechanical engineering; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Fifth level of mechanical engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you a map at some convenient point in a few minutes, but just to summarise for Their Honours' benefit. Confirm for Their Honours if this is right. Gorazde is a municipality on the south-eastern slopes of the Jahorina mountain and it's -- the river Drina runs through the town, and there are three bridges across the Drina in Gorazde town, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And from your recollection, though it's checkable, according to the 1991 census, there were 40.600 inhabitants in Gorazde municipality, and the ethnic structure, and say whether you consider this to be clearly wrong for you, the ethnic structure or balance was that 27 and a half thousand or 68 per cent of the municipality population were Muslims, 12.200 or 29 per cent were Serbs, and a very small number of Croats, and then Yugoslavs, Montenegrins and other nationalities or inhabitants, totalling just about 800 people. Does that accord with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No significant differences between what I've just said and your recollection; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I'm just going to offer you a description rather than painfully go to points on the map, because it's all checkable anyway. But the town of Gorazde consisted of areas distinctly occupied predominantly by one ethnic group rather than another, and then some mixed areas?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the Muslim population, which of course was the majority, was heavily concentrated in the Mahalla area of the town, where there were perhaps about 9.000 Muslim habitants?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Muslims were also living between the city bridge and what was known as the Bacci community in a mixed Serb and Muslim zone?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The remainder of the Muslim population was distributed in surrounding communities and villages and particularly Ilovaca, Berin, Mravinjas, Osanice, Novakovici, Oglecevi, Zupcici, Trebesko Brdo [phoen], Zapljevac, Ustipraca, Kopaci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Serbs predominated in particularly villages of Podkozara, Dubiste [phoen], Biljin, Povrsnica [phoen], Borak Brdo, Ranjen [phoen], Glamoc, Gornja Brdja, Podhranjen.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the majority of Serbs in Gorazde lived in the heart of the town itself, so the actual town was majority Serb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Mixed. But quite a few Serbs used to live in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in that region of municipalities, including Ruda, Visegrad, Foca, Cajnice, Rogatica, Kalinovik, Gorazde in that time, I'm talking about the beginning of 1990s, was economically the most developed municipality in the region, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, in the entire region, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And two particularly -- the most important industrial enterprises in Gorazde were the Unis factory at Pobjeda and a chemical plant, Azot Vitkovic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. The two biggest plants, Unis Pobjeda and Azot Vitkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that at, say, the beginning of 1990 and the middle of 1990, that inter-ethnic relations in Gorazde municipality were on the whole harmonious?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had there been some disruption of that harmony in the early 1980s?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: In the beginning of the 1980s, some extreme Muslim groups came along, and according to the public security services at the time, they were described as extremist activists and some members of those groups of Muslim nationality were found in possession of weapons and they were sent to prison for that offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: For what sort of term of imprisonment? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I don't know. Those were all crimes and it was all in line with the criminal law of the former Yugoslavia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You don't remember what sentences they got?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: They got prison sentences, but I can't remember correctly for how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you remember the names of any of the men - let's assume they were men - who were convicted?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I'm finding it difficult to remember the names. I know some first names, some surnames, but I can't really say the exact first and second name of everybody in that group. But that can be found in the official documents of the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the public security services, and that documentation certainly exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let me offer you some names. Imam Agokurovac [phoen]? Was that one of the men?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And a clock-maker called Safet Efendic? Was he one?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. The family name is certainly correct, but I can't remember the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So Efendic is correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What about Imam Hasanbegovic? Did anyone of that name have any part in any of these events?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was his part?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I think he was at the very top of that organisation. His wife was a doctor, a paediatrician, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you at the time have any personal knowledge of what they -- the purpose of that organisation was or their policies?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No. Except for what I read in the papers, because it was widely reported in the papers, and also, you know, for well what the system was at the time. Certain things were allowed to be published and others not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In brief, what was reported as the purpose or the policies of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I don't know what their purpose is -- what the purpose of their association was, but when the group we are referring to was first discovered, they were found to possess some infantry weapons. At least, that's what I heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any repetition or recurrence of such -- first of all, such Muslim activities throughout the rest of the 1980s?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, after that group was discovered, well, their activity, if I may say so, was association for enemy activity. That's what it used to be called at the time. Well, so there was this one group, and afterwards I had no knowledge of anything similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there any corresponding or similar Serb activities at any time during the 1980s in or around Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: If we can call it like that -- well, it was characteristic of the system in which we used to live, in which we lived until 1990. At the time when this group was discovered, the group that we've just mentioned, the public security service tried to strike a balance, and in the vicinity of Rogatica, they discovered that on the occasion of a christening of an Orthodox priest's son, Serb traditional songs were being sung for that act of singing Serb traditional songs. That Orthodox priest was given a prison sentence and it was a prison sentence of four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that particular event of the arrest, imprisonment of that priest, was that thought in the locality of Gorazde to have any connection with the Muslim activities and convictions that you mentioned a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No. It was engineered by the system, the former system. If you had nationalism on one side, they absolutely had to try to and find something on the other side in order to try to strike some kind of balance. That was very basis that made the system possible and made the possible for the system to continue to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I want to jump right forward to June 1990, Mr. Stavnjak, and I'll lead you on these basic facts. In June 1990, the SDA, a predominantly or entirely Muslim party, was organised in the locality and municipality of Gorazde, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then in July 1990, a municipal committee of the SDA was established in Gorazde, headed by Mr. Hadzo Efendic, who was an economist employed at the Gorazde post office?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you -- did you know of the formation of that SDA municipal committee at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. There was the initiative committee and then later on there was the municipal committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge yourself at the time of the size and composition of those committees?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I don't have any particular knowledge. I know that the president of the SDA was Mr. Hadzo Efendic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he was somebody whom you knew personally and with whom you had a good relationship, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. We were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And at that time, in the middle of 1990, there was still harmony between the different national or ethnic groups in Gorazde, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. One can say that there was harmony in the ethnic relationships, until the moment the ethnically based parties were formed, first amongst the Croats and then amongst the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When did the Croats -- the Croats formed an ethnically based party in Gorazde, did they?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I was referring to the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Gorazde, there was very few Croats. There were only 99 of them, according to the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I want to clarify. So to get it straight, the Croats did not form a local group or a local party; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, the Serbs in Gorazde, I'll say you, because you were one of them, of course, Mr. Stavnjak, began to organise themselves politically on a day known as St. Pantelejmon's Day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. On St. Pantelejmon's Day, on the 9th of August, 1990. The Serbian people in Gorazde established their Serbian Democratic Party, and I was elected a member of that committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in fact, on that day there was a quite large meeting in front of St. George's church in Donja Sopotnica, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was the municipal committee of the SDS for Gorazde formed on that very same day?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No. The municipal committee was established a month later, sometime between the 8th and 10 September 1990. This happened at the football stadium in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So there was another meeting, was there, at the stadium of the Radnici or Radnicki soccer club, attended by around 5.000 people on that date in early September 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in fact, you personally were either in charge of or in charge of the organisation of that meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the organisation committee to hold the assembly of the SDA [as interpreted], and I was the chairperson of that assembly and I announced all the speakers who delivered their speeches at that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, SDA has appeared in line 10. Whatever the witness said, whether it's a slip of the tongue, it plainly must be SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's accepted, unless the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] SDS, it should be, the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that meeting would be fairly described as the founding convention of the SDS in Gorazde; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. And for that reason, sir, I am giving you the full name of the Serbian Democratic Party in order to avoid the mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. And Dr. Radovan Karadzic was present at that meeting, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he spoke?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you to give us verbatim what Dr. Karadzic said as if you could remember, but would you be able to summarise for the Trial Chamber the key points or tone of what Dr. Karadzic said to the meeting on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: If you'll allow me, in a nutshell, I can tell you this. I don't know whether I will interpret his words well, but Dr. Karadzic said at the time that neither the Serbian nor the Croat nor the Muslim mothers would bear children that would lose their lives for the state and its organisation. In order to organise a state, one has to use brains and not human lives. The Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in Gorazde, of course, because he delivered this speech in Gorazde, sought equality, as would be given to the other two ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The civil, the ethnic, the economic, the religious, and the cultural equality, that is. Mr. Karadzic also said on that occasion that after the elections, the first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a partnership government would be established, which means, in Bosanski Petrovac, if Muslims won 15 per cent of the seats in the government, the Serbs would give Muslims more participation in power in Petrovac by as much as, for example, the Serbs gain seats in the municipality of Kalesija, or some other municipality in which the Serbs won 15 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just going back to a moment to your own position. Could you just summarise for the Trial Chamber the reasons why you were chosen as the secretary of the SDS in Gorazde in the summer of 1990.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Of course I will tell you. My parents brought me up in a very patriarchal family, in an Orthodox family. We followed the laws of the Orthodox Church. Throughout all my life, an Orthodox priest visited my house, thanks to my parents, of course. My father served with Orthodox priests for 20 or 25 years. He accompanied them in the performance of their duties in the Gorazde diocese. That's why I was considered, if you allow me to say that, an honest man that people could trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the person chosen as the president of the SDS in Gorazde was a Mr. Begovic; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stanoj Begovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He was someone you knew, maybe three years younger than you, something like that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. He was three years younger than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he was thought to be a good choice because he was an educated man, he was a law school graduate, he was not married and was therefore supposed to have more time and energies to devote to the political activities. Those were all considerations, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. He had a degree in law and I believe that this was the decisive factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just to summarise: The Serb positions held in the municipality of Gorazde immediately before the multi-party elections which came in 1990, if I just summarise these for you and confirm whether it's correct: Serbs held the position of president of the Executive Committee of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And regional police chief, and that was for the region that included Gorazde; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was the president of the Municipal Assembly at the time was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And as far as that position of regional police chief was concerned, there was an understanding that it alternated, so the post was held immediately before the multi-party elections by Mr. Stanko Stojanovic, a Serb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stanko Stojanovic was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: His predecessor had been a Muslim, but then that person's predecessor had been a Serb, and so on?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, in late 1990, after the multi-party elections, did you attend any sort of SDS meeting outside the municipality of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. After the elections, I attended one meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was that in Pale?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: That was in the Koran Hotel in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And how precisely, if at all, are you able to date that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I believe that the meeting was held in the first half of December 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you attend that meeting with your colleague Mr. Begovic, from the Gorazde SDS?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He's alive, by the way, now, isn't he, Mr. Begovic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were you the only two representatives of the Gorazde SDS who attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And had you been invited by someone on behalf of the SDS from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, from the leadership of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Krajisnik who issued the invitation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember who it was?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Somebody from the secretariat of the party, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: About how many people were at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: At the meeting there were approximately 300 people from all the municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least two representatives of each of the municipalities. We're talking close to 300 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All SDS?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. They were mostly presidents of the municipal boards, their secretaries, and vice-presidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Dr. Karadzic there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And presided over or chaired the meeting, did he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. And he held a keynote speech. And then his associates took over from him and chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember specifically any other key members of the SDS who were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I believe that the main thing on the agenda was the implementation of the results of the elections held on the 18th November 1990. The president of the Executive Board of the party, Mr. Ostojic, was there, who was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Vojislav Maksimovic there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether Mr. Maksimovic was there, but I'm sure that Mr. Ostojic was the one who chaired the meeting throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Mr. Nikola or Professor Mr. Nikola Koljevic was there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you saying you remember or that he was -- are you saying he was there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I think he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What about Mrs. Biljana Plavsic? Was she there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether Mrs. Plavsic was there. I can't remember. I've given it a long and hard thought, but I can't remember whether she was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the time of this meeting, did you know who Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik was?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No. I only heard of Mr. Krajisnik in the media when he was elected the president of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you see him on television at some point?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. From the moment when he was elected president, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you say whether the first time you saw him on television was before or after this meeting at the Koran Hotel?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I can't remember when the first session of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina took place. If you have that information, you will know. I first saw Mr. Krajisnik on TV when he was elected president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the day when I saw him for the first time on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember -- again, briefly, please, at least in the first place. Do you remember anything that was said by Dr. Karadzic to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic greeted all the attendants. He congratulated all the members of the municipalities, i.e., the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party, for the results that they had achieved in the first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And he asked them to carry out the executive power on the partnership basis, which meant cooperation with other political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it possible for you to describe very briefly what you remember as being the tone of Dr. Karadzic's remarks to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Not after such a long time. However, I can say that this was a normal conversation and this was advice to all of us, because we were all beginners in the politics, who had been elected to the positions of executive power. He advised us how to execute our power, how to talk to our partners from other political parties in our respective municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, was the physical layout of the meeting that the main body of the participants was sitting in rows, facing a top table, whether it was at a particularly higher level, a top table at which were Mr. Karadzic and some others? Was that the layout?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How long, roughly, did the whole meeting last? First of all, was it a single day?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: The first part that we all attended as a plenary meeting lasted somewhat shorter. The second part was much longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the second part took a different form, then, did it? Did you break up into working groups or task forces?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. We were split into task forces. One task force was composed of the municipalities that won less than 30 per cent participation in the municipal power. The second task force was composed of the municipalities that won between 30 and 50 per cent. And the third group was composed of those who won up to 70 per cent -- 75 per cent. And the fourth group consisted of those municipalities that won over 75 per cent of the participation in power. This is where all the municipalities were given directions, depending on the level of their participation according to the result that they had achieved in the multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So your municipality of Gorazde, where you had obtained somewhere between 26 and 28 per cent of the vote, so you just fell within the first of those groups, the less than 30 per cent group; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is this correct: That Gacko municipality was a mirror in the sense that the Muslims in Gacko had obtained a very similar percentage of the votes to those obtained by Serbs in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And there was an internal SDS agreement that the Serbs would, in forthcoming negotiations with Muslims, ask to receive the same level of participation in Gorazde as the Muslims should obtain in Gacko?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, in other words, is this right: The Gacko Serbs were going to have to give something on their arithmetical entitlement to help you in Gorazde to obtain more than your arithmetical entitlement?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you and your colleagues from Gacko had discussions on that day, at the Koran Hotel with a view to that concerted balancing arrangement?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was this all preparatory to anticipated meetings with your -- particularly in your municipality, your Muslim counterparts?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you attend any other large or non-local SDS meeting after that meeting in the Koran Hotel and before the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: After that meeting at the Koran Hotel, did you return to your home in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And meetings were then held with your Muslim counterparts in Gorazde to discuss power-sharing, were they?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did those meetings begin before or after the Serb Christmas?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: After the Orthodox Christmas of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And on the Serb side, the negotiations were led by Mr. Begovic and the vice-president, SDS vice-president in Gorazde, Mr. Mladen Mojevic [phoen], and you participated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And on the Muslim side, the leader was Mr. Efendic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you have several meetings?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: There were four to five meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How long, typically, the meetings?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: On average, two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you, the SDS, ask for the Serbs, did you ask for the Presidency of the municipality Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On the footing that the Muslims or the SDA would be able to put their person into the position of Municipal Assembly president?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Because the first person in the municipality is the president of the municipality, and the second-ranking person in any municipality is the head of the Executive Committee of the municipality. That's the hierarchy of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you ask for -- the SDS representatives, did you ask for other posts in addition to Presidency of the Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Of course. We, the representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party, asked some of the sectors, the urban planning, the others, and there were four such departments, and we wanted the head of one of these departments to be a Serb, and that's what we were entitled to, according to the results of the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What were the -- what did the SDA indicate in those discussions they were prepared for the SDS to have?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, the SDA representatives suggested some kind of deputy chairmanship in some part of the executive branch of powers, deputy chairman of an executive committee, and it was an unpaid post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that satisfactory to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No. SDS disagreed, and so we remained adamant that we should get as much as we gained at the elections in the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, according to your evidence so far, the post of president of the Executive Committee, which was being asked for by the SDS at those negotiations, was a post which had been held by a Serb immediately before the elections. Was there any difference between the post before the election and the post after the election?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Before the elections, the president of the Executive Committee of Gorazde was a person of Serb nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I didn't phrase the question very well. Leave aside the holder of the post. Was there any -- if you had had a Serb in that position after the multi-party election, would that, for all practical purposes, have been the exact equivalent of the position before the election, where a Serb had been president of the Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Now I do understand what you meant. Before the multi-party elections, the Serbs in Gorazde who had key positions of power used to be appointed by the municipal committee of the Communist League. Now, the difference is this: After the multi-party elections in November 1990, the positions of power occupied by Serbs depended on the votes cast by the Serb people in Gorazde, and therefore depended on the amount of trust that the Serb people in Gorazde had in those people. That was the essential difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In these negotiations that you were conducting with your Muslim counterparts, did you SDS leaders in Gorazde receive any instructions from the central SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Nothing but the agreement reached at the Koran Hotel in Pale, that is to say, to ask for 30 per cent of positions of power, the executive branch, that is, in Gorazde. So if you go through the list of jobs, the president of the municipality, heads of various departments and all that, so out of that total we wanted 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the result of those meetings and negotiations between you and your SDS colleagues and Mr. Efendic and his colleagues?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Those were very difficult talks. They were very tough. There was no agreement at the end. And with hindsight, I think one could say that the political parties are to blame, and in this case, the SDA party in particular, because they had absolute power in the local parliament, and they gave no indication of even a little bit of tolerance in order to try and reach some kind of agreement and for a fraction of that executive power to be handed over to the SDA -- SDS, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Efendic personally, what sort of a negotiator was he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, he was the one who was the main negotiator, and he was a tough cookie.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you date the point at which the negotiations broke down?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I think early spring 1991, the beginning of March 1991, so even earlier. At that stage, the negotiations broke down completely and the first assembly was held, and the Serb representatives did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're talking about the first Gorazde municipality assembly after the breakdown; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stavnjak, you worked at that time, didn't you, yourself, at the Pobjeda plant?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And there were about something not far short of 4.000 employees at that plant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the activities of that plant, did they include or consist of the manufacture of weapons, weapons and explosives?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, it was just the manufacture of explosives. Weapons were not manufactured at Pobjeda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you say what was the ethnic balance of the employees at the Pobjeda plant at the time we're talking about, in early 1991?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: In terms of percentages, if we look at the overall number of employees at Pobjeda, there were about between 51 and 52 per cent of Serbs, and the rest were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were a production technologist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there any changes affecting the work-force at the Pobjeda plant from the beginning of 1991?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning of 1991, the SDA started to take over both the power at the municipal level, the political power, but also in companies and production plants, and that referred to Pobjeda as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And how did that day by day and specifically affecting the work-force of the Pobjeda plant, how did that show itself?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to try and keep it brief. First of all, the general manager was replaced and then the department heads, quality control and production departments, and at the very end, even the guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I think his name was Mr. Borko Krunic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've referred to names and replacement. Was this process that you described, did it -- was it related in any way to the different ethnic or national groups in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I haven't quite understood your question. But all the management posts at the Pobjeda company at the time, whoever was a Serb was let go, and they were replaced by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes. I'll be very specific. The general manager that you referred to as having been replaced, he was a Serb, was he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. The general manager was Boro Josipovic, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hope there's no objection to my leading at this point in the evidence. And he was replaced by a Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hasan Tafro was appointed and he is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the guard whose name you think was Mr. Borko Krunic, he was a Serb and he was also replaced by a Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I just can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He was a guard or a watchman; is that a fair label on his job?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there any significant events in 1991 relating to materials at the Pobjeda plant?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Since as I've mentioned before, slightly more than half the work-force at Pobjeda was there, and the taking out of explosives and explosive devices was noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it noticed by you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I myself didn't see it, but quite a few employees commented on it at the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who did you hear was taking out explosives and explosive devices?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Explosives and explosive devices -- well, at the time, Serbs did not know who was taking them out. It was mostly employees of Muslim nationality, in fact, that were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there an incident in Gorazde in 1991 - outside the plant, I'm talking about - was there an incident involving an explosion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did that take place in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In Sandzak -- this is a hard one. Sandzaki Brigade Street, or bridge street, perhaps it is. You can probably put us right on the name of the street.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. We could say that that was the explosion in the centre of town at the Sandzackih Brigada Street. That was the name of the street at the time. And that's where the explosion took place. And at that stage, Serbs in Gorazde realised that those rumours and claims about the explosives and explosive devices having been taken out of the Pobjeda manufacturing plant were true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were two people killed in that explosion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. On the occasion of that explosion, two people were killed, a man and a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were they occupants of the flat or apartment where the explosion took place?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: The woman used to live in that flat, and the man did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the name of the man who was killed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I think, if I remember correctly, his name was Dzafer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there an official explanation offered for the explosion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: According to what I heard, the information from the public security station in Gorazde, headed by a Muslim, said that a gas container had exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that explanation accepted by the local population?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Serb people in Gorazde did not bite and they knew full well what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What did they know?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: The Serb people knew that it was caused by the explosives that were talked about and that originated from Pobjeda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the woman who was killed, what -- had she been employed immediately before her death?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. She used to work at Pobjeda, and she dealt with explosives and explosive devices in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In 1991, do you recall any noticeable changes of activity relating to JNA reserve officers in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I think they gradually started to absent themselves from work during the time when they were still employed at Pobjeda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you say "they," are you talking about JNA reserve officers of all ethnic nationalities and groups?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: We're talking about the former JNA reserve officers who were Muslims and who used to work at Pobjeda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of any reason why they had started to absent themselves from work?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: According to the information from citizens of Serb nationality, from Ilovaca, those former reserve officers of the JNA of Muslim nationality used to go to Ilovaca for training, military training. utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, was there a point at which you and Mr. Begovic withdrew from active politics in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. In the second half of 1991, Mr. Begovic and myself withdrew from the leadership of the Serb Democratic Party and we were replaced by Mrs. Miroslava Herin, who was a doctor, and Mr. Bosko Sekaric. And Mr. Mojevic stayed on as deputy president.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say the second half of 1991. Are you able to be any more precise than that about the date when you ceased activities?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date, but I do know that it was in the second half of 1991. I know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was Professor Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Professor Kosoric was an inspector of schools at the republican level, and when my party activity came to an end, he withdrew as well. When Mr. Begovic and myself withdrew, Professor Kosoric withdrew as well, and we set up a Serb cultural association called Prosveta, and it was in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What specifically did Professor Kosoric withdraw from? What position or activity?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Professor Kosoric was a member of the municipal board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stavnjak, you yourself owned a property at that time between Gorazde and Cajnice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. My father and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you or your family, then. You owned an apartment in Gorazde and then you or your family more than one property between Cajnice and Gorazde; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you personally knew SDS leadership in Cajnice?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you receive any information about any connections between Muslim leaders or political activists in Cajnice and Muslim leaders or political activists in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. According to my knowledge and according to what I heard from my colleagues from the Serb Democratic Party from Cajnice, there was indeed cooperation between the SDA and the Cajnice and the SDA in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did that cooperation manifest itself in any specific action in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. By the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, some Muslim extremists, an extremist group, broke into the warehouse of the agricultural cooperative called Sloga, or Unity, at Cajnice, and they appropriated some infantry weapons, that is to say, some rifles. And it was the cooperative that owned those rifles, and so that was within the framework of the Territorial Defence, the system that was still in existence in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, sometime in the spring of 1992, did you personally on some occasion run into a difficulty about obtaining petrol for your car?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. By the beginning of March, there were fuel shortages in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was there any specific occasion when you first ran into particular difficulty yourself?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. If you went to a petrol station in March 1991 and you asked for petrol, the attendant would just tell you that they were out of any fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This happened to you, did it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that as far as you were aware at the time -- it's just drawn to my attention by my colleague. You said if you went to a petrol station in March 1991. You mean 1992, do you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: 1992. It was March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were told that the -- well, you were told on one -- at least one occasion that the petrol station was out of fuel, were you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, was that true?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: As far as I know, there always used to be fuel at the petrol station, but it was denied to the representatives of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What nationality was the pump attendant who told you -- I think I've made an assumption there. What nationality was the person who told you that the petrol station was out of fuel?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you able to obtain petrol fuel from any other source?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, or as of then, I myself and all the other Serbs in Gorazde who needed petrol for their cars had to travel between 50 and 70 kilometres away from Gorazde in order to fill up. So that in some instances, we went as far as Pljevlje in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You had a big enough tank to get there and back, did you, Mr. Stavnjak? Did the same problem affect Muslims?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell the truth. Some Muslims were not in a position to get fuel, which made me think that there was rationing of fuel in Gorazde, with a view of certain things to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So did it affect some Muslims, or was the Serb and Muslim community affected equally by this problem?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Some Muslims, of course, were affected, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I think I'll have to put the question specifically to you again. Were the Serb and Muslim communities affected equally by this problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps then also add to that the source of knowledge for that specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly. Also knowledge for the question, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll put the question -- so there's no misunderstanding, I'll put the question to you first again. I hope it's coming across to you all right, actually, in translation. Were the Serb and Muslim communities affected equally by this problem of obtaining petrol?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No, no, not in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what was the difference?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Not a single Serb could get fuel, and a minority of Muslims were unable to get fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was this something you were able to observe personally or information you obtained from somewhere else, or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I personally observed this, and also in conversations with other Serbs who resided in Gorazde at the time, they told me that none of them could obtain fuel from the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And your knowledge of the relative difficulties for Muslims in obtaining petrol, was that from your own observation or from some other information, or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the petrol station in Gorazde, which is still there, there were some Serb houses, houses inhabited by Serbs, and they could observe what I have just told you, and they told us who was entitled to petrol and who wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock, although I haven't quite finished on petrol. This would be as convenient a point as any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it would take more than a couple of minutes, then we'd better have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It would, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say, in case it's helpful, that it does rather look as if I'm going to be quite close to my original estimate rather than my revised estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a message which is mainly of importance for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Well, I'm transmitting it across the courtroom in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, was there then an incident involving supply of petrol to a Serb in Gorazde which then triggered off rather more action?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And could you briefly describe what you know about that incident and what happened.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Sometime around the 11th of March, I believe it was the 11th of March, 1992, one of the Serb citizens of Gorazde whose family name was Radovic came to the petrol station to fill up. There was no fuel for him, just like there was none for other Serb citizens, as we have already described. And when the worker at the petrol station told him that there was no petrol for him, this gentleman called Radovic tied a rope around the petrol tank or petrol pump. He tied this to his car and pulled the pump out of its mount. This act, this incident, was the first incident -- at least that's how it was qualified, as an inter-ethnic incident in Gorazde. It had a huge impact. On the same day, Muslim citizens of Gorazde blocked the roads and streets in the town. This was done by some of the Serbs as well in the areas where they made up a majority. This blockade of roads and a huge level of excitement among all the citizens of Gorazde lasted for three days. After those three days, special units arrived with armoured vehicles. They were members of the republican secretariat of the interior. There were talks between representatives of the Muslim people, on the one hand, and the Serb people, on the other hand, and one can say that after these three days, the situation calmed down to a certain extent. During those three days, in the evening hours, one could hear sporadic shots from the village called Pargani. I could tell where the shots came from because my apartment is directed towards that village, the apartment in which I resided at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This would be a convenient point at which to show you a map of Gorazde, Mr. Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I handed up a batch. It's black and white copies. We were very helpfully provided with a coloured map from which it's taken. I think this one's going to be adequate for our purposes, I think put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you intend to tender that map in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would be convenient, Your Honour, because it will tie in with the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D89, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know -- can we bring it up? Gorazde is in the middle -- well, it's to the left. It's the left-hand edge, about -- well, just below halfway down at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you zoom in?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, please. Could we zoom in? The witness can help to point out where Gorazde is. If we could zoom in on that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would already zoom in, Madam --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the left-hand side of the map you can see Gorazde, at least on the map that I have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you referred to what you regarded as being the source of that gun-fire. Could you try to -- perhaps you need a slightly finer implement to do it than the one with some knob on the end. Perhaps a simple ballpoint pen or something like that would be better.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I have a pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please refrain from writing unless specifically instructed to do so. So you can point -- yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So my question: You referred to the source of -- what you regarded as the source of the gun-fire. Can you point to where you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. This is left to Kazagici, next to the Drina River. This is where it was. The village of Pargani, you can't see it here, but it's a rather big settlement, composed of Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps, with respect, would it be convenient if the witness did mark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may instruct him to do so. Just to prevent --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. Thank you very much. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would you just mark with -- let's start with an X in this case, and just mark with an X where on the map that place is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for one second. One second, please. Didn't we have a colour code? Blue for the Prosecution and black for the Defence? Was that it? Yes. That means that marking on the request of the Defence should be done in black, so that we later can identify. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Colour it black is the phrase of today, Mr. Stavnjak. Would you mark with an X, please, where you say on the map that place is.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You had referred to checkpoints or blockades, I think was the word you used. I'm afraid, I'm sorry, I introduced the word "checkpoint" there. You referred to blockades. But-- I'll lead, Your Honours. Were the blockades of roads following that incident about the protest at the pump, were they in the nature of checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Those were checkpoints, where you could see armed civilians of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you said armed civilians of Muslim ethnicity. You did indicate a short while ago in your evidence that there were blockades by both ethnic communities. Was there a sequence of blockades or checkpoints by one ethnic group and then by another ethnic group, or did it all spring up simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: As far as I know, according to my information, that is, there was just one checkpoint at which Serbs expressed their outrage with the incident involving petrol, and that checkpoint was somewhere around the Orthodox church. I believe that the name of the settlement where this happened was Rig [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was that the first response, then, to the incident, or was there an earlier response by any other group?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I said that there was just one checkpoint, which was put up by the Serbs. They were guarding their church in the settlement called Rijeka. In the entire town, there were some dozen of checkpoints held by the Muslim people. So during those three days, almost the entire town was under the control of the Muslim population of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did those incidents give you any information or knowledge that you had not previously had about the availability or prevalence of weapons in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I had reliable information. On the first or second day out of the three when the complete town was paralysed, I went to a shop to buy some food. At a distance of some hundred metres from my apartment, towards the food store, there was an armed Muslim civilian holding a rifle in his hand, who just waved his hand, indicating to me not to approach him. Of course, I returned to my apartment, and after these three days were over, I decided to evacuate my family from the apartment, which was no longer safe. The thing that had happened was a warning to me. At that time I had two young children. My older son was 7. His name is Nikola. And my younger son, Stefan, was 3. I put them in my car. The blockade had been over by then. And I drove them towards Cajnice, together with my parents. I took them to our weekend cottage in a place called Miljen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we look again at that map -- it should be still up on the ELMO, or perhaps it can be brought back. Yes, it's there. Now, just to get it straight: The Drina River is flowing broadly northwards, north-east, isn't it, through Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so we can conveniently refer to the west of the river as the left bank and the east of the river as -- in Gorazde as the right bank. That would be conventional for you, wouldn't it, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. The Drina flows from south to north, and as you look downstream, we always called this the left bank and the other the right bank. The Drina flows through the city centre, so the town is situated on both banks of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the place to which you evacuated your family, Miljeno, is about -- is south-east of the centre of Gorazde, about -- well, on the map it's about 10 centimetres or something like that south-east.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I'm pointing towards this place called Miljen. Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then was there, after the events you've just described with your wife and sons being moved, did you have some subsequent difficulty in crossing the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I evacuated my family from our apartment. I took them to Bare. Here you see it. Bare was mostly populated -- actually, it was of mixed ethnicity, but Serbs were a majority. And this is where my wife's sister had her house. And this is where they were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Bare is --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: This was in the second half of March and the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we can see that Bare is on the right bank of the river. Did you then -- a slight repetition, but you didn't give a specific answer. Did you subsequently have a particular difficulty in crossing the Drina River from the left bank to the right bank?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to tell you about this. I was going to tell you what happened next.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: When my wife and my children remained at my wife's sister's house in Bare, which is in the suburbs of Gorazde, I would occasionally go back to the apartment. I would go to work at the Pobjeda company. I would then return to this house in Bare, and that's where I would spend nights. One day, I believe this was sometime in mid-April, I went to my apartment in my car to take some food that had been left there. Together with me in the car were Mr. Marko Krunic, my sister-in-law's husband, and Mr. Nikola Koljevic, who was a teacher at the secondary school in Gorazde. We went to my apartment in my car. My apartment was on the left bank of the Drina. And we set off from the right bank of the Drina. I parked my car in front of my apartment. I went to my apartment and collected some food items there. I spent only a few minutes in the apartment. When I returned to the car and went back, since my apartment is close to the first bridge on the south -- actually, on the north. There are three bridges on the Drina in Gorazde. The northernmost bridge is the closest to my apartment. The distance is only about 50 metres. I wanted to cross that bridge. The two aforementioned gentlemen were with me --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I just pause there, Witness. I know, and it isn't going to be a mystery. We're going to talk about three bridges. I wonder if, please, you could just mark them B1, B2, and B3. Could you write that on the paper. It's not a very large-scale map, but if you could just mark those bridges, starting from the north, please. If you start from the northernmost bridge, just mark them as closely as you can B1, B2, and B3, before we go into what happened on the bridges.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you so much. Let's, then, start with what happened at B1, the first bridge.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: When I arrived at the B1 bridge in my car, as I wanted to cross from the left bank to the right bank of the Drina River, I was intercepted by a police car. The road was blocked across the bridge. There were some reserve policemen in uniform and some policemen there. They didn't say anything. They just waved their hands, showing to us that we should go back. I returned to the centre of town because the bridge B2 is in the very centre of the town. Normally there was no traffic across that bridge. It was mostly a pedestrian bridge. On that bridge as well, there were reserve policemen in uniform and civilians. I could not cross that bridge either in my car. I continued along the left bank of the Drina up to the B3 bridge, in a place called Bacci. When I arrived there, as I wanted to turn towards the bridge, I, that is, the three of us, came across a large group of people composed of Muslims, some 20 of them altogether. They all held rifles in their hands. One of them, who had an automatic rifle - I could see that because we were that close - ordered me to step out of the car, not only me, but everybody who was in the car. We got out of the car. They asked us if we had any weapons. We obviously said we didn't have any. We opened the trunk. Only Mr. Marko Krunic said that he had a weapon because he was an active policeman and he had a pistol. The man who held a rifle in his hands said, "Okay. You can go now, but never come back this way." That's how I managed to cross the Drina, across the B3 bridge, and I returned to Mr. Krunic's house. After that, having realised what the situation was and having understood the message that this man gave me as we were crossing the bridge, I packed my wife and children and I took them to Miljen, which is some 10 kilometres off Cajnice. I believed that my children would be much safer there. I was clear at that point that their safety in Gorazde would have been threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In April 1992, did any difficulties arise in Gorazde in relation to food availability and distribution? We're leaving the map now for the moment, Mr. Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in mid-April -- actually, in the second half of April, the companies in Gorazde worked on and off. The events that had taken place in the month of March up to mid-April threatened the safety of all citizens, especially of Serbs. That's why the companies worked on and off. The managers who were mostly Muslims distributed food that had been obtained with the money that the companies had in their accounts at the time. In the second half of April, there was such a distribution of food, and I must admit that even some Serbs got some of that food. However, when you take into account that all the managers who were involved in the distribution were Muslims, this points to the fact that most of the foodstuff ended up in the hands of the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could I just ask two clarifying questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of them is the following: You said you took your wife and children to Miljen at a certain distance of Cajnice. Was that outside of the municipality of Gorazde? Did you leave the municipality of Gorazde and then -- because I cannot see on this map where the borders are between Cajnice and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took my children and my wife to a place called Bare first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a second. Because Bare we now learned is close to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had difficulties in crossing the bridge. You took them to Miljen or Miljeno; I can't see correctly. Is that within or outside of the opstina of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miljeno is within the municipality of Cajnice and is just outside the municipality of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question would be: Did you then return to Gorazde or did you stay with your wife and children in Miljeno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I went back to Gorazde, and I stayed at my sister's and brother-in-law's house, the Krunic family. Because it was in the month of April and I was still working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were -- you went back to Bare. You did live in Bare and not in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you said that after the blockade, you said: [In English]: "After three days, special units arrived with armoured vehicles." [Interpretation] Could you tell us what exactly it was about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After three days of total blockade, special units from the republic secretariat for the interior came along. I don't know who they were exactly, but special forces belonging to the police at the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they had an armoured vehicle and it was parked in front of the police station in Gorazde. And then they organised talks between the two peoples and then the blockade was lifted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how many individuals were there, roughly speaking, how many of them were there from those special forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. All I know is that two or three combat or rather armoured vehicles arrived, but I'm not familiar with the details and I did not participate in these talks, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see them, those men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you see the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I did see the vehicles. They were parked in front of the police station in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were they lorries or special vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Special armoured vehicles, armoured police vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, was there a violent incident in the region of -- or in the municipality of Gorazde on the 8th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
