utterances.text: At that stage, the tragic conflict in Gorazde had already broken out, and in a village called Borak Brdo, which is situated to the north of the town, extreme Muslim units entered that village, Borak Brdo, set everything on fire, and killed eight Serb civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you please indicate, returning to the map, please could you indicate on the map where that happened. We might need to scroll up a bit.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Borak Brdo, I think it says on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It might be helpful for the record, Mr. Stavnjak. Could you just write against that "8th May" -- oh, no, don't worry. Just -- we'll leave it. It's not going to help, because of languages and so on. We've spotted it. Perhaps put a ring around the name of that place, please.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you referred to extreme Muslim units, could you explain, please, what you mean by that description, "extreme."

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the armed individuals who officially had not been armed before, because officially the JNA was still in existence. So there were some paramilitary units, or extreme armed paramilitary formations, since they managed to kill eight individuals of Serb nationality in that village. It seems to indicate that they must have been armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did that extreme group, as you've described them, did they have any name or label under which they went?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of what did or might have triggered off that particular violent incident?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I don't know about the causes, but that was the epilogue. Those Serbs in the village of Borak Brdo were killed, I mean the Serbs that were caught in the village. Mostly those people were elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know any of their names?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I know one name, Branko Gladanac. I'm sure about him. And I'm not very sure about the others, so I wouldn't venture any names here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could we ask the witness, because he gave a lot of answers in relation to this incident, how he learned about it. Did you see it yourself? Did you hear it? If you heard it from someone else, who was it? When did you hear it? So to give us better insight on the source of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It came out later. We found out from the Serbs who were on the left bank of the Drina. At that time, I was on the right bank myself. So half the Serbs were on the left bank, because they used to live there anyway. Since war broke out in Gorazde on the 4th of May, citizens of Gorazde, the Serbs in Gorazde, had no idea when it would happen, and it happened on the 4th of May, and those who found themselves on the left bank stayed there, and those who found themselves on the right bank stayed there. So this incident on the 8th of June on the left bank of the river Drina is something that we found out from the citizens who were in the area, and I was in touch with them, and they told me about it later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they tell you that they had been eye-witnesses or did they see the results, or what was the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just the results. I don't suppose anybody was left alive. No eye-witnesses were left alive. Everybody was killed and the entire village was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, just to clarify. You referred to the 8th of June just a moment ago. Just so that we can be clear: You've talked about 8th of May and 8th of June. Which was the date of this incident?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: The 8th of May. I do apologise. I did say the 8th of June, but in fact it was the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's no problem, Mr. Stavnjak. I just wanted to clarify. Was there, subsequent to that incident, then, on the 8th of May, was there some sort of incident in a village near Vitkovici?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. After that, and I can't recall the exact date because that part of the territory around Vitkovici and Vitkovici itself was under the control of the Muslim forces. What should be underscored here is that in a place called Crkvina, which is not marked on the map, and it is in the immediate vicinity of Vitkovici --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, can you show us Vitkovici? It's easy to find, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's pretty much due south. Scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Vitkovici was on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. If we could just scroll down, please, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It comes into sight. Again, perhaps you could just put a ring around Vitkovici.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the village that you mentioned, that I won't even attempt to pronounce, to save the interpreters, that's very close to Vitkovici, is it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: If I may -- well, I marked it with an X, the place called Crkvina. Now, there were two Serb families in that village. They were called Delic and Zmukic. 18 members of the Zmukic family and the Delic family who happened to be in their houses at the time were taken to an unknown place and they are still missing today. Let me just stress that an elderly woman who died last year was called Bozana Delic, and on that occasion four of her sons were taken away and nobody knows where they ended up, not to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you personally know any of the Delic or the Zmukic family?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I personally knew Radivoje Delic, who was one of the four sons of Mrs. Bozana Delic. He worked for the same company where I used to work, at Pobjeda, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When is the last time you remember seeing him?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: At some point in mid-April, at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you ever seen him since?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What is the basis of your knowledge of what you've just described in relation to the Delic and the Zmukic families?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, my basic knowledge is -- well, we can say that the Serb people in Gorazde experienced an enormous tragedy. Large numbers of Serbs were killed or are still missing to this day. Let me just stress that Gorazde, at the centre of this upper Drina region, which had six municipalities, Rudo, Visegrad, Gorazde, Cajnice, Foca, Kalinovik, was an area which, as I said, had Gorazde as its absolute centre. And just in the municipality of Foca had more citizens of Serb nationality than of Muslim nationality. The second one in this respect was Gorazde, and that makes this tragedy of the Serbs in Gorazde all the greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any sort of - at this time - any sort of camp in Vitkovici or in the area of Vitkovici?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have more precision in terms of the date the witness is talking about, when this camp referred to existed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, at this time. I'm sorry. I had intended to mean exactly the time I was just talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So May 1992, was there any sort of camp in Vitkovici or in the immediate vicinity of Vitkovici?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, according to what I heard from Serbs who remained on the territory held by Muslim units, Mr. Momo Carapic and a cousin of his called Milivoje Carapic, well, they spent a period of time in Gorazde, starting from the breakout of this tragic conflict up until 1994 or 1995. So more than two years. They spent more than two years down there in Gorazde. And they told me -- I mean, they live in Cajnice, and this is where I live at the moment as well. And they told me that one of those collection centres for Serbs was situated at Vitkovici at the old printworks, somewhere in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And from what you heard, was it already there in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Straight after the breakout of that tragic conflict and the first days of war, all those inhabited areas, villages, houses, inhabited by the members of the Serb people, were rounded up and they were taken to those smaller collection centres, such as the ones that Mr. Momo Carapic and Mr. Milivoje Carapic went through. They went through that, and I think they were exchanged, and that's how they survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you used the phrase which comes across as collection centres, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: What I mean is that from the start of the tragic conflict in Gorazde, there was no place left for Serbs there anymore. In other words, Serbs could not continue to live in Gorazde and stay alive. Their very livelihood was at threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've referred more than once to the outbreak of the conflict on the 4th of May, 1992. What actually happened on that day, on the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: On that day, there were some shooting incidents. The shooting mostly came from the Muslim areas and were directed at the areas inhabited by Serbs, and the other way around as well. So at the very start -- well, it is a bit difficult to describe how it started, in much the same way as the incident in relation to fuel, when there was shooting for three days. At that stage it was only at night, and on the 4th of May, it never stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you hear shooting yourself on the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, I was at a place called Miljeno because the 6th of May is St. George's Day and it is a holiday in my family, and so I went up there in order to prepare for the holiday and because it is the patron saint of my family, so I was at Miljen that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that's the place that we looked at before about -- well, on the map it's about 10 centimetres. I forget precisely what the scale is. That's the place south-east of Gorazde that we see on the map, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think it's about 10 kilometres away from Gorazde, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking, 10 to 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So were you too far away that you didn't hear the gun-fire yourself then; is that correct, on the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, but I heard of it. And I heard that this was the way in which that tragic conflict started. And at that time, the 4th, the 5th, and the 6th of May, I was at Miljen and Cajnice. And if I could just explain, because my family, my parents, my children were there. We all gathered together. It is a traditional custom for the Serbs, for the whole family to get together on the day of the patron saint.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there a point in 1992 when Serbs, for whatever reason, left Gorazde in significant numbers?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Later on, at around -- on the 26th and the 27th of August, 1992, all citizens of Serb nationality who found themselves on the left bank of the river Drina left their homes and went in the direction of Rogatica. I'm going to try and find Rogatica on the map, if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we can see that fairly easily, can't we? It's at the very top of the copy we've got.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Slightly to the east of due north of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think we needn't worry about marking. That's really terribly easy to find. Thank you. What you've described of the citizens on the left bank leaving their homes and going in the direction of Rogatica, that was coordinated in some way, was it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No. There was no organisation of any sort. But I must stress one event which took place when these people were leaving their traditional homelands on the left bank of the river Drina. In a place called Kukavice -- let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's about eight -- six centimetres due south of Rogatica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. In a place called Kukavice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Put a ring round that one, please, Mr. Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]. In a place called Kukavice, there was a very tragic event that took place there, and Serbs who were running for their lives at the time -- I mean, we are talking children, women, and the elderly, and they were killed in a bus. We still don't know the exact number of those killed, but there is still a monument which was erected there with names and surnames of all those killed in the village of Kukavice on that day. It was a village which was under Muslim control. All of them were civilians, women, children, and the elderly, about 30 people in all. Amongst the killed was my uncle, Milisav Stavnjak, and his wife, Andja Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And do you know who killed them?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I don't know the names, but they were killed by members of extremist Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What's the basis of your knowledge of that incident and those killings?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, those were Serbs whose lives were threatened, and they were withdrawing towards Rogatica. Rogatica was not very safe either. There was conflict there as well. But they felt it would be safer, and they were on their way to Rogatica through these villages and across the hills. And when they got to Mesici, I think they got on a bus there. There was a bus there at Mesici. I think the driver is still alive. This is an interesting piece of information. I mean, the driver who was driving all those people, he was shot in both legs. But even so, he managed to get the bus as far as the territory which is safe for the Serbs. And I think his family name is Jagodic. Just a moment. I will remember his family name exactly. He's certainly still alive. I think he is now living at Foca or Rogatica. And I can easily find out what his name was. He was driving the bus at the time, and he was shot in both legs but he survived nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you hear about this incident at any time from people who claimed to have witnessed it first-hand?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you how I found out about it. Since my family was in Miljen and Miljeno and Cajnice were swept up in this tragic conflict, my children were at risk once again, and I took my children to Belgrade, and at that time, on the 26th, between the 26th and the 27th of August, St. Mary's Day, 1992, when I took my children to Belgrade, I found myself in a place called Uzice, in Serbia, where there were lots of Serbs from the right bank of the river Drina. From Gorazde, they were sitting around in the park in Uzice and I heard from them about everything that had happened. And there were other close relatives of mine, other uncles and aunts, one other uncle and aunt survived, fortunately. So that's all I have to say about that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've talked about the -- described Serbs living on the left bank in Gorazde leaving and going north, in the direction of Rogatica. Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber what proportion of the Serbs living on the left bank in Gorazde left at that time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the percentage. However, however many Serbs found themselves on the left bank at the time, they all left the territory of Gorazde on the left bank of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What happened about the Serbs living on the right bank of the Drina?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: A total exodus of the Serbs of Gorazde took place 20 days after the event that I have just described. This was on the 18th and 19th of September, 1992. The Serbs who were on the right bank of the Drina, in the town and in the suburbs and settlements around Cajnice, they all left their homes and set off towards Cajnice. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. On the 19th of September, 1992, Gorazde became an ethnically clean town, cleansed from the Gorazde Serbs. Only a few individuals remained in the town in their apartments, but here we're talking a very insignificant number of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what is the basis of your knowledge about what happened, as you've just described, to the Serbs living on the right bank of the Drina?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: The two that I have just mentioned, Mr. Carapic, Momo and Milivoje, resided on the right bank of the Drina in a village called Bucje. They were taken to prison, according to them. That's what I learned in a conversation with them. They had been taken to prison and they spent some time in that prison up until 1994, when they were exchanged. But as I've already mentioned, quite a few Serbs in Gorazde are still considered missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There is -- well, I'll rephrase that. What happened to the church of St. George in Donja Sopotnica, which is in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: The only Serbian Orthodox church that existed in Gorazde was downstream from the Drina, some two and a half kilometres off the town. The St. George's church in Donja Sopotnica was destroyed sometime around the 1st of September, 1992. In other words, three or four days after the Serbs left their homes on the left bank, the church itself is on the left bank, it was destroyed, and on that same day, the parish house was also destroyed, the parish house was the home of the Gorazde priests. This house was in the centre of the town of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The church is Donja Sopotnica -- is that more or less in the same place as what we see on the map as Sopotnica, just slightly to the north-east of the town of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: If we go downstream the Drina River from Gorazde, this is where you see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We're going far downstream here. If we scroll the other way. We've got to get it straight. Downstream is up the page and up the map to the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Going down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. We can stop there, I think. We're just above where you're indicating is the name Sopotnica.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The church is, well, in the near vicinity of where we see the name Sopotnica on the map, is it, or was it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. The church was immediately next to the main road, in the very proximity of the main road, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you just put perhaps "SG" would be useful, for St. George. Just put "SG" where the church is.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I expect [indiscernible] -- but I don't think that would cause any problems at all. Thank you, Mr. Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I won't ask you to mark in the centre of town because it's -- well, it's not going to help very much probably, given the map. I'm sorry, did you wish to add something to your answer?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: If I may. I used Cyrillic, but in respect of the Court and the audience here, I used Latinic in combination with the Cyrillic. So one letter is a Cyrillic letter and the other is a Latinic letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: A man of compromise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a nice compromise. I fully agree. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were any mosques or other Muslim buildings in the municipality of Gorazde destroyed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. There were a lot of mosques in the territory of Cajnice. In the town itself there was just one, but in the suburbs and in the surrounding villages, there were quite a lot of them. None of them were destroyed on the territory of Gorazde. I was talking about the church, but I omitted saying that it was set to fire. In 1994, the security services centre of Srpsko Sarajevo brought criminal charges for the destruction of that church, which was under the protection of the state. It was a very important historical monument, because it used to house the first printing shop in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: From the sixteenth century; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, from the sixteenth century. The church itself was built in 1463, so it was a fifteenth century church.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just to clarify. I asked you whether any mosques or other Muslim buildings were destroyed in Gorazde, and you answered by saying: "Yes, there were a lot of mosques in the territory of Cajnice." So you moved municipalities. And then you said that: "None of them were destroyed on the territory of Gorazde." So please, could I just ask for clarification. In 1992, or indeed after 1992, first of all, were any mosques or other Muslim buildings destroyed in the municipality of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Not a single mosque on the territory of Gorazde was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what about 1992 or afterwards, so far as you can say, in the territory of Cajnice?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: On the territory of Cajnice, a few mosques were destroyed. I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, this is right, is it: You did national service in the JNA in 1981 in Zagreb and Rijeka, both in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were -- then you were a reserve squad leader, a JNA reserve squad leader; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you joined the VRS shortly after its formation. You joined on around the 20th of May, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you weren't conscripted; you voluntarily joined; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were an infantryman throughout your time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the JNA -- the VRS, I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: From the end of May to the end and the signing of the Dayton Accords. In practical terms, I stopped serving in the VRS on the 1st of April, 1996, when, after the Dayton, the number of staff was reduced. That's how my service ended on the 1st of April, 1986 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you have a uniform from the first day that you were in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No. No. I wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I think a moment ago, it's drawn to my attention, the transcript said 1996. I'm not quite sure what you said. You said your service ended on the 1st of April, 1986. You must have meant 1996. Or perhaps you said 1996, but confirm that it ended April 1996.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: 1st of April, 1996 is when my membership in the VRS ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, both dates the first time, 1996, the second time, and apparently a mistake, 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It's all cleared up now, anyway, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Back to your uniform. You say you wore civilian clothes. When did you subsequently acquire a uniform, a VRS uniform, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Sometime towards the end of August or beginning of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When was the -- change of topic now, Mr. Stavnjak. When was the first time in your life that you met Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: As I've already said, I first saw him on TV as president of the then Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I believe that your question is when I actually saw him in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Stavnjak -- we see lots of people on television we've never met, I'm sure. I do mean specifically when you first met him personally, yes.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I met Mr. Krajisnik for the first time towards the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: In Cajnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the occasion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: It was in late autumn 1994. The occasion was opening of the road. The Serbs could not travel because the roads had been cut off, and the only road that they could take was towards Pljevlje, in Montenegro. The Serbs then built a road towards Ustipraca, Miljeno and Cajnice. The section between Ustipraca and Miljeno was constructed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just stop you there, Mr. Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that there were reasons why a new road had to be there. I think Mr. Stewart is mainly interested in meeting Mr. Krajisnik and what kind of, if any, conversation you had with him. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's exactly right, Your Honour. May I go straight to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The meeting you had with Mr. Krajisnik, was it just a handshake or was it a few words or was it a long chat or what? Please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik came to Cajnice for the first time on that occasion. That's when I met him. I shook his hand. And the occasion was opening of the section of the road. And why was Mr. Krajisnik in Cajnice? I can say before this Trial Chamber that he had some emotions about Cajnice because his wife was a native of Cajnice. Her family hailed from the area. Their family name is Miletic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Micevic. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you had some sort of pleasant short chat with Mr. Krajisnik; is that -- say if that's the wrong description or confirm that it is.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: There was a large group of people. Mr. Krajisnik was with that group, representing the government of Republika Srpska, at that time, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I myself was a member of the local authorities of the municipality of Cajnice, and as such, I was invited to attend the opening of that section of the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, we saw on the 65 ter summary that there has been other occasions, at least that's what you expect the witness to testify, other occasions where he met Mr. Krajisnik. If there's any reason to believe that he had any substantive conversations with him or anything else that might shed a different light on what we have heard until now, we'd like to hear that. If not, we'll just accept that. I don't know whether on the Main Board meetings whether there was any subject matter which needs further attention. So I'm not preventing you from doing it, but just to establish that frankly words were exchanged that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm more than happy with that, and perhaps I can just wrap it up by saying this:

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You met Mr. Krajisnik in 1997, 1998, at SDS Main Board meetings, by which time you were yourself a member of the Main Board; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I was not a member of the Main Board at the time, but I did go there because I was the deputy of -- the member of the Main Board from Cajnice and I was the one who attended those sessions in 1997 and 1998, and I saw Mr. Krajisnik at those sessions. Our last meeting was in 1998 in Cajnice at the pre-electoral rally for the interim parliamentary elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when Mr. Krajisnik was a candidate for a member of parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, just a couple more points. I just want to return to something which I had actually omitted from some time ago in your evidence. Just going back to the power-sharing discussions that you had in Gorazde with your Muslim counterparts. You'd referred to a link between your municipality and Gacko at the meeting at the Koran Hotel. When you were having your power-sharing negotiations with the Muslims in Gorazde, were you in touch during that time with your SDS colleagues in Gacko?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No. We just had telephone conversations in order to find out whether they had agreed on establishing the local authorities in Gacko and things to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, we supplied a document with a view to its being an exhibit, and there's a very short schedule of exhibits with just two items on it. Your Honour, the thing to say about the first one is it's been very recently disclosed to us under Rule 68. In the circumstances, Your Honour, there's simply no practical possibility- I apologise - of our obtaining a translation into English of this document, which is in B/C/S or in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I wonder how a mainly English-speaking Prosecution could identify the -- I don't know what kind of Article 68 disclosure it was, whether it was exculpatory or not. But if so, then one would at least expect the Prosecution to know to what extent it is exculpatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only assume the Prosecution have resources, B/C/S resources, of which I cannot dream. That's all, Your Honours. I suppose they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, this is -- perhaps we could just first of all be clear what this is. The heading -- perhaps if you read the first two or three lines of the heading, then we shall get a translation of it. That's the easiest way of doing it. So where it says Srpska -- Yes. Mr. Sladojevic suggests that I should give the ERN number. It's ERN 00596529-33, for the record. Mr. Stavnjak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar -- I take it that you want to tender this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D90, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, would you just read the first -- before you get to those dates, just read the first couple of lines of the heading of this document and then we'll all get the translation then through the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read slowly, because otherwise the interpreters couldn't follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before me, I have a document that I have never seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies. I was just checking whether that had happened. I'm sorry. In all the rush, we did omit that. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: But I'll try and read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just want a heading at the moment, please, so we can ...

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party is the heading. The War Presidency of the Serbian municipality of Gorazde, number 02-163/92. Date: 11 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then perhaps you could just go to the end of the text, where you see -- just turn over the page. You see a name as the person ostensibly who issued this document. Could you read that little chunk there with the name and title and so on.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: This document was signed on behalf of the War Presidency, because on the 11th of May the tragic conflict had already started in Gorazde, and the president of the War Presidency was Mr. Stanko Stojanovic. He is the one who signed this document. I know the gentleman personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You gave us a bit of editorial there, Mr. Stavnjak, but the Trial Chamber will appreciate that that's what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm very nearly at the end with this and the other exhibit, so may I, therefore, ask the Trial Chamber's indulgence. It would be convenient, I suggest, if I ask the witness to read this document, even though it is a couple of pages, and then we will get the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And to read it aloud at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just looking at the clock. We could still do that before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, sorry. Would you do that, please. Would you just read the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- text of this document, and the interpreters, who I think now have a copy - yes - will deal with it. Thank you to them as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have read out the heading. The document is addressed to the Muslim people of the municipality of Gorazde. The Muslim Assembly of the municipality of Gorazde. And it's regarding response to the warning. "We have received a warning from the president of the Muslim municipality of Gorazde, whom the Serbian people do not recognise as president, nor do they recognise his authority. In the text of the wording, the so-called president has accused the Serbian leadership and the Serbian people of the aggression and the beginning of conflict, which is far from the truth. He probably counts on the fact that the defence of the Serbian people, according to his criteria, equals aggression and that the Serbian people do not have the right to defend themselves. "The general public of Gorazde is familiar with the fact that the representatives of the Serbian people have invested a maximum effort in order to reach an agreement on the division of the municipality into the Serbian part and the Muslim part of the municipality, and also in order to establish two separate sets of authority, by which peace in Gorazde would have been preserved. "However, all of these agreements have been obstructed by the leadership of the Party of Democratic Action. By their policies and by their pursuit of power, they have brought the Serbian population of Gorazde into a degrading position. They have introduced the rule of terror and ill-treatment, and they have forced them to flee the town and to organise their self-defence. "However, even that was not enough. So that the Muslim extremists from the ranks of the Green Berets, the Patriotic League, and the HOS, under the auspices of the leadership of the Party of Democratic Action, started attacking Serbian villages and killing innocent citizens, by which they started an act of aggression and assumed responsibility and blame for the outbreak of this conflict. "Ludicrous ideas, borne out of extremists have brought about chaos, in which the citizens of Gorazde find themselves at this moment. And this criminal act has shown that they are consistent in implementing the genocidal policy against Serbs by taking away and denying their right of self-defence. This shows that the talks that they engaged in with the Serb side were a sheer farce and a lie, intended to hide criminal intention. "The Serb people is well familiar with the activities of the SDA extremists and their plans. We have at our disposal the proof to show that a certain number of high-ranking representatives of the municipal authorities and the SDA participated in the preparation of such acts. The general public is soon going to be informed of all that. "Due to this policy pursued by the SDA leadership in Gorazde, innocent citizens, both Serbs and Muslims, suffer. Many of them are forced to flee to safety outside Gorazde, and very often staying with Serbs in Serbia, and that selfsame political leadership described those Serbs as the enemies, the sworn enemies of the Muslim people, the democracy, quote/unquote, advocated by Hadzo Efendic in trying to fool the Serbs, has now shown its true face. There was no place for the Serb people in such a democracy, no place for them as people with equal rights in this municipality. We are addressing the Muslim people in this way and appealing to them to renounce the policy engaged in by Hadzo Efendic and his entourage, in the interest of all citizens of Gorazde, and to appeal to them to reject the armed extremists and to force them to surrender their weapons in order to create the preconditions for the suspension of the conflict and the setting up of democratic power and authority. "Otherwise, the agony which has befallen Gorazde is bound to continue, an agony which has become unbearable for all our citizens. The Serb people will never accept any ultimatums or threats coming from Hadzo Efendic, and shall never accept his absolutist power. It will continue in a defence of their age-old homes, their pride and dignity, at all costs. "The very warning issued by Hadzo Efendic contains a clear threat to innocent captured citizens of Serb nationality, to women and the elderly, who his fighters found in their homes and who are being taken to unknown locations. It is a threat that unless Serbs accept his ultimatum, they will come to grief, unless they accept the ultimatum and subject themselves willingly to his tyranny. "In this warning, he also announces broad-based action against the Serbs. This is the best proof of his so-called good intentions and the so-called welfare and well-being that is on offer to Serb people. The Serb people does not use, and shall never use, such methods of blackmail because it is not the way we do things. At the same time, we would like to stress that the Serb people, throughout history, has never been frightened by blackmail and ultimatum, not even when they came from higher powers than Hadzo Efendic and the likes of him. "We hope that the Muslim people will find it in themselves to remove the leadership which has dragged them in this sort of situation, because they are the main cause of the conflict. We hope that honest and deserving men will be found to lead the Muslim people and lead it out of this blind alley that Hadzo Efendic has taken it to on the basis of his policies, and that the right men will be found in order to reach agreement with the Serbs, in order to build a peaceful, democratic life, which would be in the best general interest of all of the inhabitants of the municipality of Gorazde. "The War Presidency and the president Mr. Stojanovic Stanko" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would just like to point out this is not normally the way we do things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm aware of that, and it should be avoided at any cost. At the same time, I first of all would like to compliment the witness. I think he's the first one who read two pages in such a space, that at least you could follow, but I fully agree that this is not the way in which interpretations should be presented. So therefore, it might need some more thought on how to proceed in the near future with these kind of documents. I can't resolve it right away now, but we'll pay attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we say, we hardly subscribe to that. I must say, of course, I don't know the Serbian, but the English translation sounded extremely smooth and coherent. So from a pragmatic point of view, Your Honour, we -- I suggest it would seem that we could now dispense with the step of having a formal translation, unless either party or the Trial Chamber suggested it were a necessary step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to give that some thought, because that would deviate from the Appeals Chamber, if an Appeals Chamber ever has to look at this, would be in a position where they would have to listen to the -- or to read the transcript rather than to have the document in front of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's why I was suggesting, Your Honour, unless there were any objection from anybody concerned, that that could be taken as the -- well, Your Honour has the point. I am grateful to the interpreters. I hope Your Honour appreciates that the time-scale of the material being disclosed and then our being able to handle it and so on has led us to this position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be less than five minutes, but I don't know whether that five minutes is more conveniently dealt with now or after a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say it's less five minutes, I would, as a matter of fact, continue and then see how far we come today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, thank you for that. With all that, I simply would like to ask you this: Is there -- did you see -- have you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness said already that it was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, if that was already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May we note that what you've been reading, in fact there's a handwritten document. It appears to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We noticed that attached to the typed out version there's a handwritten document which, at least as far as the beginning and the end is concerned, says exactly the same in handwriting. I take it that the parties will have a look at it, whether it's the same. I don't know what's the use of two different versions of the handwritten document and the typed-out document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I dare say, Your Honour, that was what was disclosed to us and probably we haven't got to the bottom of that, but it may be not be too difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear if there's anything special.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, is there anything in that document as you've been reading it that, from what you know, you would say is wrong?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I wouldn't say. I just read through it very quickly. If I may, I would just like to comment on one point. This fits in, so to say, with what I said in the beginning of the afternoon, that is to say, that those talks with Mr. Efendic were very difficult and tiresome and that there was no agreement in the end. So those people who followed in my and Mr. Begovic's footsteps in the SDS in Gorazde were unable to reach any agreement at all and that's why this tragic conflict broke out. Of course I would like to say that Mr. Efendic, or rather, the SDA in Gorazde, bears most responsibility for this tragic conflict, because the responsibility is always in the hands of those who have absolute power. And at the time, it was the SDA which had absolute power in Gorazde, so they had to show some tolerance, and I think that they really are to blame to quite a considerable extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is there anything in this document which you've just read which you would say was unfair?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No. I have nothing to say about the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, therefore -- thank you very much. I'm handing up one other document. It's the last one. It's the -- well, I'm handing up. I hope a copy will come from somewhere else. It's the second item on that, well, list of two, Your Honour, tab 2, ERN 00495337.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Stavnjak, I'm just going to read from that schedule. This is described as an order by Radovan Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May I just intervene for just a minute. This is already an exhibit. It's Prosecution Exhibit 690.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was quite familiar to me, because it says how it was distributed, wasn't it? Each municipality, how the communication took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's extremely helpful, Your Honour. It saves an extra exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No. This is the first time, today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon, could you give us an indication of how much time the Prosecution would need for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would say, Your Honour, in the area of an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that means that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's a rough estimate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then at this moment, Mr. Stavnjak, we'll have a break for another 25 minutes, then continue for approximately half an hour today, and then we hope to finish tomorrow not too late in the afternoon. Yes? We'll adjourn until 25 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On my screen, it says that we're in private or closed session, but I'm not aware that we are. But perhaps it was the computer monitor which said "closed session," and not the video monitor, which I should have looked at. Mr. Harmon, you've got 25 minutes today. I was informed that we also would need five minutes on scheduling issues, as far as I understand, at the end of this hearing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to start, Mr. Stavnjak, first of all by showing you a map. This is a map, Your Honour, that comes from Prosecution Exhibit 527. And if that could be placed on the ELMO. This map, for Your Honours' benefit, locates Gorazde in relation to other municipalities that had been the subject of testimony in this case. I thought it would be of benefit to Your Honours to see a copy of this map. Mr. Stavnjak, do you have a copy of that map in front of you or to your side? If you turn to your side, there's a map on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if the usher could put the area of Gorazde, Cajnice, Foca, Sarajevo on the map -- on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, we can see from this, very quickly, that the municipality -- Mr. Stavnjak, we can see from this particular map that the municipality of Gorazde is between the municipalities of Foca, Sarajevo, Rogatica, Rudo, and Cajnice. My first question is: Can you tell the Court how far Gorazde is from the city of Pale?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Ninety kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how far is it from the city of Cajnice?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Twenty kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And from the city of Foca?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Thirty-three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And from the city of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: From Rogatica, about 30 kilometres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we could turn to the next exhibit, which will need an exhibit number, and that is an item that is in the upper left-hand corner entitled Gorazde and bears the ERN number 00482241.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would have number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P965, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I am corrected. I am told that this is part of the census that we have distributed to Your Honours. So this should be, then, P954. So I stand corrected. We don't need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I see that it's in the end of -- it doesn't need a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It doesn't need a number, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 965 is now free again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the reason I exhibit this for Your Honours and Mr. Stavnjak is because in your direct examination testimony, Mr. Stavnjak, you provided to this Chamber statistics relating to the number of Muslims and the number of Serbs who inhabited Gorazde municipality, and you gave the figure of 12.200 Serbs who inhabited Gorazde and 27.500 Muslims inhabiting Gorazde. This map, if you take a look at it to your left, Mr. Stavnjak, is based on the 1991 census, and it puts the figures as follows: The number of Croats at 80, the number of Serbs at 9.843, the number of Muslims at 26.296. Do you accept those to be the accurate figures from the 1991 census, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly I can agree, because yes, the number of Muslims seems to be correct. The number of Serbs is slightly less here. Because probably some of them said that they were Montenegrins or Yugoslavs or whatever. But roughly speaking, I can agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The numbers of Yugoslavs who identified them as such was 789 and the number of people who identified themselves as others, according to this census, was 565. Now, Mr. Stavnjak, if you could actually take this exhibit in your hand and examine it, you will see that this exhibit identifies with various dots in the colour green, colour blue principally in Gorazde. Green identifies the Muslim hamlets and blue identifies the Serbian hamlets. And this is, again, based on the 1991 census, Mr. Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I bring that to the Court's attention just for information purposes. Your Honour, the next exhibit is not going to be shown to the witness. It's presented to Your Honours and to counsel because -- and it's this exhibit here that is in the same format as Exhibit 527. The reason I submit that to Your Honours is because there has been some testimony about streams and rivers, the River Drina, for example, certain roads, and this document, Your Honours, clearly shows those particular geographic features that might be of interest to the Chamber and might come up in the course of the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It even shows some villages we couldn't find on the other map earlier, Pargani, for example. And it is one of -- I'm always very unhappy with these distorted pictures, but let's try to live with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This needs an exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P965, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Is it not one of the maps we had -- no, no, of course not, because it's Gorazde, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. As I say, it's presented to Your Honours perhaps to assist the Chamber in identifying features more clearly than from other maps that the Court has at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, you testified in part about the Pobjeda factory, which in part manufactured explosives; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that the only factory of military significance located in the Gorazde municipality or were there others?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. This was a military fabric, a military company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And as such, Mr. Stavnjak, that particular plant had strategic significance to the potential combatants in this war; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony, in part you testified about some extreme groups in 1980. One of the groups you said was an extreme Muslim group, and you testified that there had been some arrests as a result of that particular group. Do you know -- can you tell us more about that group than you've testified about? Was the prosecution of this group because it was a group that was anti-communist and represented a threat to the existing order?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I've read in the papers, criminal procedures were instituted against that group and it was proven that they were engaged in the enemy activities. Some weapons were mentioned. This is what I know. In any case, there is a complete file on that case on the files of the then public security services of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get a clarification from you, Mr. Stavnjak. I take it from your evidence you don't know much about this particular group, based on your personal knowledge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No, personally I don't know much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like you, Mr. Stavnjak, to turn your attention to a meeting that took place in late 1990, following the multi-party elections, a meeting that you attended at the Koran Hotel in Pale. And what was the purpose of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: The purpose of that meeting was to invite all the leaders of the party at the local level of the Serbian Democratic Party and to reach an agreement on partnership with other political parties in all the municipalities. That was after the first multi-party elections had taken place in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your evidence, you gave a very detailed structure about how the groups were to divide power, and you broke -- according to your evidence, you broke into task forces those groups that where the Serbian Democratic Party had received less than 20 per cent of the vote, and you went through to a point where a task force was created for groups that went over 75 per cent of the electoral vote. Now, when you attended the meeting that your task force, which Gorazde fell into, which was less than 30 per cent of the vote, was there a general discussion about how the power and the positions in the municipality were to be divided, or was the group in which you were a participant informed that there had been earlier discussions between the higher-level leaders, Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Kljuic, Dr. Karadzic, about how the positions were to be divided in municipalities, depending on the electoral vote?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I personally attended those talks as a representative of the municipality where we had less than 30 per cent of the vote. Mr. Ostojic, who was the then president of the Executive Committee, gave us that instruction. He told us to seek the position of the president of the Executive Board and one of the departments, and that is if we won less than 30 per cent of the vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So Mr. Ostojic was the person who came to your group and essentially told you what positions you needed to try to get in your municipality, a municipality where the Serbs had won less than 30 per cent of the vote?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, precisely what I've just told you. He told us to try and get hold of the position of the president of the Executive Board, and depending on the number of the departments in a given municipality, we were told to ask for 30 per cent of those departments as our participation in the local power-sharing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When Mr. Ostojic told you what positions to seek, do you know if his instructions were the result of other discussions that had taken place between Mr. Kljuic, Dr. Karadzic, and Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic was speaking on behalf of the SDS Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your testimony, you said that: "All municipalities were given directions, depending on the level of participation and the results of the vote." Did your municipality, you, Mr. Stavnjak, and other representatives, then follow those directions that had been given to you by the SDS superior body?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, within the Serbian Democratic Party, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was it normal for the municipal authorities to follow the directions given to them by the higher levels of the Serbian Democratic Party? Was that the standard operating procedure?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, yes. However, the situation was different in various municipalities. In practical terms, this was very hard to implement, if not impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Stavnjak, was: In your municipality, did your municipality follow the directions given to it by the SDS higher-level authorities, as you did in the meeting that took place at the Koran Hotel?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Basically, we adhered to that, but this was not decisive for the final outcome of the process of agreeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand. My question is somewhat different, Mr. Stavnjak. My question is: This is an example, is it not, of an occasion where the SDS party in your municipality were given directions and you followed them? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. We can say that these were just principles. But in reality, it was very difficult to implement that. It is very difficult to weigh the weight of any position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in general terms, and not necessarily relating to this example, when the SDS higher-level authorities gave directions to the municipal authorities in your municipality, it was the practice in your municipality to follow those directions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: I would say that this would be true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you think of any example when the SDS higher-level authorities gave a direction to a member of an SDS board -- I'm sorry, the SDS party in your municipality that was not followed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know there's going to be an issue raised in the last five minutes, and at this point it would be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stavnjak, we have to deal with a procedural matter. Therefore, we'll stop now. We'd like to see you back tomorrow, and I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak to anyone, Prosecution, Defence, friends, family, whoever, about your testimony, the testimony you've given today and the testimony you're still about to give tomorrow. Then we'd like to see you back. I take it, Mr. Registrar, the same courtroom. Same courtroom, quarter past 2.00 tomorrow. And I'll invite now Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I hope it won't be a difficult issue at all. Your Honour, the next witness that the Defence are proposing to call is a Mr. Djordjevic, no protective measures are being sought. The plan had been for him to begin his evidence first thing on Wednesday morning. He does in fact arrive this evening. I should tell Your Honours that. It's clear that we're going to be a little while longer with this witness tomorrow, but not the whole day. Your Honour, the position is this: That, if I may say, it's entirely acceptable and in many ways suits both Prosecution and Defence if we stick to that original plan and start on Wednesday morning. But of course we wanted to make sure that that had the approval of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand that this has been a matter of discussion with Mr. Stewart and Mr. Tieger and that's satisfactory to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. I mean, of course, the Court - that's not a surprise - is not entirely happy that we've got only two witnesses this week, but scheduling might need some more attention. But given the fact that we have two witnesses this week and not anyone else, then there's no problem that we'll stick to the original schedule. At least, assuming, Mr. Stewart, that we'll finish this witness this week. I don't know -- I have not clearly in my time how much time is scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That shouldn't be difficult, Your Honour. And may I say I accept the general remark Your Honour has made and am grateful for the Trial Chamber's endorsement of that procedure for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn until tomorrow morning, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
